paragraphs: It is explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, zal, in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, page 61, and this is his language: You must also know that although it was explained above that during the meal, on a weekday, one should feel sorrow in his heart — especially if he is alone — over the Destruction, as mentioned in the name of the Zohar; nevertheless, in Birkat HaMazon (the Grace after Meals) one must, on the contrary, show extra joy in his heart. The reason is that the matter of eating pertains to the supernal attribute of Malchut, which is nourished from the flow of Tiferet, and through the intention we direct in our eating we draw down flow and sustenance to it, and from what we draw down to it, it in turn distributes and gives sustenance to us. Therefore one must bless Birkat HaMazon with a generous eye and not like the mean of eye, etc. — until here his language; examine it there. Therefore every person should be careful to bless Birkat HaMazon with joy, with a glad heart, and with great intention, and if he has no cup in hand, his hands should be bound one over the other on his chest, and he should close his eyes and bless with intention, just as our teacher, zal, wrote.

clarification.explanation: The Ari wrote that although during the meal itself, on a weekday, it is fitting to feel some sorrow over the Destruction, in Birkat HaMazon itself one must, on the contrary, show extra joy in the heart. The reason: the matter of eating belongs to the attribute of Malchut, which is nourished from the flow of Tiferet, and through the intention of our eating we draw down flow and sustenance to it, and from what it receives it distributes and gives to us; therefore one must bless Birkat HaMazon with a generous eye and not with a stingy eye. Therefore every person should be careful to bless Birkat HaMazon with joy, with a glad heart, and with great intention. And if he has no cup in hand, he should bind his hands one over the other on his chest, close his eyes, and bless with intention.
takeaways: Birkat HaMazon is recited with joy and a generous eye (unlike the sorrow appropriate during the meal itself)
Without a cup: hands clasped on the chest, eyes closed, with intention

paragraphs: Our teacher the Rashash, zal, wrote in his siddur, and this is his language: Before Birkat HaMazon one should intend to prepare himself to fulfill the positive commandment of blessing Birkat HaMazon with awe, with love, with tremendous intention, and with great joy and a glad heart, in order to draw down abundant flow and blessing, and mochin (supernal illuminations) and vitality and sustenance to the holy Malchut of Atzilut, and from her to us and to all the holy worlds; and he should close his eyes and bind his hands one over the other, the right over the left, as one sitting before the King, the King of the world, the holy Malchut of Atzilut. It is further written there that one should intend that he is ready to fulfill the positive commandment of the Torah to bless after eating, as it is said, "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless," etc. — and through this preparatory intention, there will be power in his intention in the blessing to raise up mayin nukvin (feminine waters) and to draw down four mochin to the aspect of Yud-Heh, etc.; examine it there.

And in my small book Mikvatzi'el I wrote a text to say before Birkat HaMazon: "For the sake of the union of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, etc. — behold we come to fulfill the positive commandment of the Torah to bless Birkat HaMazon, as it is written in the Torah, 'And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless the Lord your God for the good land which He has given you,' in order to repair the root of this commandment in a supernal place. And may it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers, that the first blessing, the second blessing, and the third blessing which we are now about to bless over the food be considered important, accepted, and desirable before You, and that You grant us strength, ability, help, and assistance to raise up mayin nukvin and to draw down four mochin to Yisrael and Rachel; and may the fourth blessing which we are now about to bless also be considered important, accepted, and desirable before You, and may You grant us strength, ability, help, and assistance to raise up mayin nukvin and to draw down four lights of mochin to Yaakov and Rachel; and may it be accounted before You as though we had directed all the intentions proper to direct in these four blessings of the Grace, 'and let the pleasantness of the Lord,' etc."

clarification.explanation: The Rashash wrote that before Birkat HaMazon one should intend to prepare himself to fulfill the positive commandment, to bless with awe, love, tremendous intention, joy, and a glad heart, in order to draw down flow and blessing and mochin and vitality and sustenance to the holy Malchut, and from her to us and to all the worlds; and he should close his eyes and bind his hands one over the other (right over left) as one sitting before the King. And our teacher, in his book, wrote a text of "Leshem Yichud" to say before the blessing, in which one requests that the first three blessings (which are from the Torah) and the fourth blessing be considered important and accepted before God, that he be granted the strength to draw down the mochin properly, and that it be accounted as though he had directed all the proper intentions in the four blessings.
takeaways: Before the blessing we prepare ourselves to bless with awe, love, joy, and intention
One recites "Leshem Yichud" so that the blessings be accepted and rise as though all the proper intentions had been directed

paragraphs: The four blessings of Birkat HaMazon have the law of the Amidah prayer, and one may not respond to them — not even Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barchu — and likewise one may not greet another during Birkat HaMazon, because of awe and honor; its law is like that of the Amidah. And if his house is adjacent to the synagogue, or a minyan was praying inside his house and he heard "Modim," he should bow his head in the direction the congregation is bowing, and upon hearing Kaddish or Kedushah he should be silent and listen, as is the law during the Amidah.

clarification.explanation: The four blessings of Birkat HaMazon have the law of the Amidah prayer: one may not respond to Kaddish, Kedushah, or Barchu during them, and one may not greet another, because of awe and honor. And if his house is adjacent to the synagogue, or a minyan was praying in his house, upon hearing "Modim" he should bow his head in the direction the congregation is bowing, and upon hearing Kaddish or Kedushah he should be silent and listen, as is the law during the Amidah.
takeaways: Birkat HaMazon is like the Amidah: one does not respond to Kaddish/Kedushah in it and does not greet others
Upon hearing Kaddish/Kedushah, one is silent and listens; upon "Modim," one bows the head

paragraphs: One must sit while reciting Birkat HaMazon, and should not bless while standing or walking unless he is traveling; nor should he recline, as this is a manner of haughtiness — rather he should sit with awe. And some say that even the blessing Me'ein Shalosh (the abridged after-blessing) must be said seated, and it is good to be careful about this in all blessings.

clarification.explanation: One must sit during Birkat HaMazon, and should not bless while standing or walking (unless traveling), and should also not recline, as this is a manner of haughtiness; rather he should sit with awe. And some say that even the blessing Me'ein Shalosh (recited after cake, wine, or fruit) must be said while seated, and it is good to be careful about this in all blessings.
takeaways: Birkat HaMazon is recited seated and with awe, not standing and not reclining
It is good to recite even Me'ein Shalosh while seated as well

paragraphs: It is forbidden to bless while engaged in one's work, even a light activity such as drying one's hands or putting on a garment and the like. And here in our city, where there is great heat in the summer months, and it is customary to fan oneself with an implement called a "marvacha" (a fan made of palm-branch leaves) on the face and body, one must be careful not to fan oneself by hand during Birkat HaMazon with this implement, since this is considered an activity — for Birkat HaMazon and the Amidah prayer are equal in these matters, and there is no difference between them except that prayer is said standing and Birkat HaMazon seated. And indeed, because of our many sins, many common people are lax regarding Birkat HaMazon, blessing it very quickly, and some engage in some activity during the blessing, or gesture with their eyes, wink with their lips, or fidget with their fingers, and the like — and one should rebuke them about this with moral instruction, and to those who listen it will be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to bless Birkat HaMazon while engaged in work, even a light activity such as drying the hands or putting on a garment. And in a place where it is customary to fan oneself on the face and body due to heat, one must be careful not to fan oneself during the blessing, since this is considered an activity — for Birkat HaMazon and the Amidah prayer are equal in these matters, and the only difference between them is that prayer is said standing and Birkat HaMazon seated. Many are lax regarding Birkat HaMazon and bless it very quickly, or engage in activity during the blessing and gesture with their eyes and fingers, and one should rebuke them about this.
takeaways: One does not bless while engaged in an activity, even a light one (drying hands, fanning oneself)
Birkat HaMazon is equal to the Amidah, and one should not be lax or hurry through it

paragraphs: It is customary to remove the knife from the table during Birkat HaMazon, and the more meticulous remove every iron implement, such as a fork and paper scissors. And the Acharonim, zal, wrote that one need not be strict about all of the above on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And in Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh, page 12, it is stated in the name of our teacher the Ari, zal, that one who is of the root of Kayin must be careful to remove the knife entirely during Birkat HaMazon, and it is not sufficient merely to cover it; examine it there. Therefore every person must be careful about this, since none of us knows his root, and so we too are accustomed to remove it even on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

clarification.explanation: It is customary to remove the knife from the table during Birkat HaMazon, and the more meticulous remove every iron implement (fork, scissors). The Acharonim wrote that one need not be strict about this on Shabbat and Yom Tov, but it is brought in the name of the Ari that one who is of the root of Kayin must remove the knife entirely during the blessing, and it is not enough merely to cover it; therefore every person must be careful about this, since we do not know our roots — and so our teacher is accustomed to remove it even on Shabbat and Yom Tov as well.
takeaways: One removes a knife (and the meticulous remove iron implements) during Birkat HaMazon
It is customary to remove it even on Shabbat and Yom Tov, since one's root is unknown

paragraphs: During Birkat HaMazon one should make audible to his own ears what he utters with his lips, and even though Maran, zal, holds that if he did not make it audible to his ears he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact, one should be stringent: if he has more bread, he should go back and eat and bless properly, so as not to enter into a doubt of nullifying a positive Torah commandment, since some say that if he did not make it audible to his ears he has not fulfilled his obligation; see Chesed LeAvraham, Siman 185, letter 1.

clarification.explanation: During Birkat HaMazon one should make audible to his own ears what he utters with his lips. And although Maran holds that after the fact one has fulfilled the obligation even without making it audible to his ears, one should be stringent: if he has more bread, he should go back and eat and bless properly, so as not to enter into a doubt regarding the nullification of a positive Torah commandment, since some say that if he did not make it audible to his ears he has not fulfilled his obligation.
takeaways: One makes Birkat HaMazon audible to his own ears
If he did not make it audible and has more bread: he should eat and bless again, out of doubt regarding a Torah obligation

paragraphs: Some say that if one ate but did not drink water, and he is thirsty, he is not obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah but only by rabbinic law. Therefore, if one ate and did not drink water and is thirsty, he should make every effort to obtain water and wait until water is brought to him and drink, so that he will bless Birkat HaMazon by Torah law; and if he cannot find water to drink, he is obligated in Birkat HaMazon by rabbinic law.

clarification.explanation: Some say that one who ate bread and did not drink water, if he is thirsty, is not obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah but only rabbinically. Therefore one who ate and did not drink and is thirsty should make every effort to obtain water and wait until it is brought to him and drink, so as to bless Birkat HaMazon by Torah law. And if no water is found for him, he is obligated in Birkat HaMazon rabbinically.
takeaways: One who ate and is thirsty but did not drink: according to this view, obligated only rabbinically
He should make an effort to drink water in order to become obligated by Torah law

paragraphs: If one ate bread and did not drink water because he was not thirsty, or he did drink water — in either case he is obligated in Birkat HaMazon by Torah law. And if he later became uncertain whether he had blessed Birkat HaMazon or not, he must recite the first three blessings, since they are from the Torah and a doubt is treated stringently; but "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," which is rabbinic, he should not bless out of doubt. And even though there are those who hold that one should bless that one as well, we maintain that a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently. The same applies if he erred in the middle of Birkat HaMazon and does not know where he erred, or he dozed off and does not know which blessing he is in — he returns to the beginning, on account of a Torah doubt, and only regarding the fourth blessing, if he is in doubt about it, he should not bless it. However, if he did not eat enough to be satiated — in which case he is not obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah — or he ate enough to be satiated but was thirsty and did not drink — in which case likewise he is not obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah — in such a case he should not go back and bless out of doubt even the three blessings, since he is obligated to bless only rabbinically; and if it is possible for him to eat anew and bless, that is well done.

Likewise, one who eats pat haba'ah bekisnin (a bread-like pastry) and is in doubt whether he blessed Me'ein Shalosh or not; and likewise if he is in doubt whether he ate a kezayit of bread or less; and likewise a woman who ate bread and was satiated and became uncertain whether she blessed Birkat HaMazon or not — if it is possible to eat anew and bless, or to fulfill the obligation through the blessing of others, all the better; and if not, they should not bless out of doubt.

clarification.explanation: One who ate bread (and was not thirsty, or drank water), and is thus obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah, and becomes uncertain whether he blessed, must recite the first three blessings, which are from the Torah and a doubt regarding them is treated stringently — but should not bless "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (the fourth, rabbinic blessing) out of doubt. Likewise, if he erred in the middle and does not know where, or dozed off, he returns to the beginning (out of Torah doubt), and only regarding the fourth blessing, if in doubt, he does not go back. But one who is obligated only rabbinically (did not eat enough to be satiated, or was satiated but thirsty and did not drink) does not go back to bless even the three blessings out of doubt; and if it is possible for him to eat anew and bless, all the better. Likewise one who eats pat haba'ah bekisnin and is in doubt about Me'ein Shalosh, or is in doubt whether he ate a kezayit, or a woman who ate and was satiated and is uncertain — if it is possible to eat again or to fulfill the obligation through others' blessing, all the better; and if not, they should not bless out of doubt.
takeaways: Obligated from the Torah and in doubt: he blesses the three [Torah] blessings, but not "HaTov VeHaMeitiv"
Obligated only rabbinically and in doubt: he does not go back; if possible he should eat again or hear it from others

paragraphs: Even though it was said that three blessings are required even in cases of doubt, behold, if it happened that one ate enough to be satiated and blessed Birkat HaMazon, and a short while later ate only a kezayit and was satiated by it because his second eating was close to the first eating — such as the third Shabbat meal followed closely by a fourth meal — the poskim were in doubt about this matter: whether this second eating is considered satiation from the Torah, since in fact he is now satiated by this kezayit, or perhaps this is not considered satiation, since the satiation results from the force of the first, adjacent eating, over which he already blessed Birkat HaMazon, and therefore he is not obligated in Birkat HaMazon from the Torah for the second eating. The same applies if he ate a kezayit that by itself does not constitute enough for satiation, and only because he ate other foods along with it did he become satiated — whether he is obligated from the Torah in this case. And these doubts have not been fully resolved; therefore, if one of these cases of doubt occurs to him in Birkat HaMazon, such that he does not know whether he blessed or not, he should not go back and bless even the three blessings, but rather should listen to Birkat HaMazon from others who are blessing properly over their own eating, and intend to fulfill his obligation, and they too should intend to fulfill his obligation for him; see Ar'a DeYisrael, entry Bet, letter 11, and Peri Megadim, Siman 184, sub-section 8, and Chesed La'alafim 184, new addition 3, and other Acharonim.

clarification.explanation: Although we said that in cases of doubt one blesses three blessings, if one ate enough to be satiated and blessed, and a short while later ate only a kezayit and was satiated by it (because his second eating was close to the first, such as the third Shabbat meal followed closely by a fourth meal), the poskim were in doubt whether this satiation obligates from the Torah (since he is indeed satiated now) or not (since the satiation stems from the force of the first eating, over which he already blessed). Likewise if he ate a kezayit that by itself is not enough for satiation, and became satiated only in combination with other foods. Since these doubts were not clearly resolved, if such a doubt occurs to him in Birkat HaMazon, he should not go back and bless even the three blessings, but rather listen to Birkat HaMazon from others and intend to fulfill his obligation, and they should intend to discharge his obligation.
takeaways: Being satiated from a kezayit close to a prior meal, or being satiated only in combination with other foods: the Torah obligation is in doubt
In doubt in such cases: do not go back, but rather listen to others and intend to fulfill the obligation

paragraphs: Women are obligated in Birkat HaMazon, and because of our sins, nowadays many young women eat without a blessing due to lack of knowledge, and they themselves, and their father, and their husbands are destined to give an accounting for this. It is fitting for every person to teach his daughter, in her youth in her father's house, the text of the blessings on enjoyment and Birkat HaMazon, at least the short version written in the books; and if she did not learn it in her father's house, her husband is obligated to teach her — all of this as mentioned in Chesed La'alafim. And I, the humble one, in our city, may it be built and established, printed the short text of Birkat HaMazon in which one mentions the special occasion on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh, to distribute to women free of charge, and many young women come and take this text printed from our house. And along with this text, I also printed an even shorter text for those who are most lax and do not know how to read the Ashurit script, so that they should at least say this in place of Birkat HaMazon: "Berikh Rachamana Maran Malka De'alma Marei Dehai Pita, Berikh Rachamana Dezan Lechulla" ("Blessed is the Merciful One, our Master, King of the world, Master of this bread; blessed is the Merciful One who sustains all") — and this short text they can learn by heart after becoming accustomed to it.

clarification.explanation: Women are obligated in Birkat HaMazon. And because of our sins, many of them eat without a blessing due to lack of knowledge — and they, their father, and their husbands are destined to give an accounting for this. Therefore it is fitting for every person to teach his daughter, in her youth while still in her father's house, the text of the blessings on enjoyment and Birkat HaMazon — at least the short text found in the books; and if her father did not teach her, her husband is obligated to teach her (Chesed La'alafim). And the Ben Ish Chai relates that he printed in his city the short text of Birkat HaMazon (which mentions the special occasion on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh) to distribute to women free of charge, and many come and take it; and he also printed an even shorter text for those who do not know how to read the Ashurit script — that they should at least say, in place of Birkat HaMazon: "Berikh Rachamana Maran Malka De'alma Marei Dehai Pita, Berikh Rachamana Dezan Lechulla," a text that can be learned by heart.
takeaways: Women are obligated in Birkat HaMazon; it is fitting to teach every daughter in her youth, and if not — the husband is obligated to teach her.
At least the short text; and one who cannot read should say by heart: "Berikh Rachamana Maran Malka De'alma Marei Dehai Pita, Berikh Rachamana Dezan Lechulla."

paragraphs: There are people whose manner is to eat slowly, and they do not eat a full kezayit measure — which is nine dirhams — within the time it takes to eat a peras, which is the time it takes to eat three eggs, that is, fifty-four dirhams. Therefore one must warn them strongly about this, that they should not delay in eating the kezayit beyond the time it takes to eat a peras, and after they have eaten a proper kezayit, they may then finish their meal as slowly as they wish. This is because many of the poskim, zal, hold that if one delayed eating the kezayit — which is the measure of obligation — longer than the time it takes to eat a peras, he does not bless Birkat HaMazon nor any after-blessing at all, and this view is primary, even though there are those who disagree — particularly since we maintain that a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently; see Zechor LeAvraham, part 3, at the beginning of the final section. And we will write more on this matter further on, God willing, in a different parashah.

clarification.explanation: There are people who eat slowly and do not eat a full kezayit (nine dirhams) within "the time it takes to eat a peras" (the measure of eating three eggs, fifty-four dirhams). One must warn them strongly not to delay eating the kezayit beyond the time it takes to eat a peras, and after eating a proper kezayit they may finish eating slowly as they wish. This is because many poskim hold that if one delayed eating the kezayit (the measure of obligation) beyond the time it takes to eat a peras, he does not bless Birkat HaMazon or any after-blessing at all, and this view is primary — particularly since a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently.
takeaways: One must eat a kezayit of bread within "the time it takes to eat a peras" (the time of three eggs)
If he delayed longer: he does not recite an after-blessing; after the kezayit he may continue slowly

paragraphs: If one ate and then vomited, and he is uncertain whether a kezayit of what he ate remained in his stomach, he has entered a state of doubt and should not bless Birkat HaMazon until he eats more, if it is possible for him to eat. And if it is not possible for him, he should listen to the blessing from others and intend to fulfill his obligation. And if this too is not possible, he should bless Birkat HaMazon without mentioning God's name and sovereignty, but should merely contemplate God's name and sovereignty in his mind and not utter it with his mouth. And this law applies not specifically to Birkat HaMazon but also to one who eats or drinks wine and vomits — the law is the same, as we have written; see the Acharonim.

clarification.explanation: One who ate and vomited, and is uncertain whether a kezayit of what he ate remained in his stomach, enters a state of doubt and should not bless Birkat HaMazon unless he eats more (if possible). And if that is not possible, he should listen to the blessing from others and intend to fulfill his obligation. And if that too is not possible, he should bless Birkat HaMazon without mentioning God's name and sovereignty, contemplating the name and sovereignty in his heart. This law applies also to one who eats or drinks wine and then vomits.
takeaways: Vomited and it is in doubt whether a kezayit remained: he should not bless unless he eats again
If that is not possible: he should listen to others, and as a last resort bless without God's name and sovereignty, contemplating them instead

paragraphs: In the first blessing one should begin thus: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, the God who nourishes us and the entire world in His goodness," etc. And so it is in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, zal, who reads "HaEl," etc. And when he says "Poteach et Yadecha" ("You open Your hand"), he should intend that the initial letters of "Poteach Et Yadecha" have the numerical value of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei (spelled as Yud-Aleph-Heh-Dalet-Vav-Nun-Heh-Yud), and he should intend that the final letters (Chet-Tav-Kaf) — and by the At-Bash cipher, Sa-Aleph-Lamed — also equal that same divine name numerically; and in the word "UMasbi'a" ("and satisfies") he should intend that it equals numerically Chet-Tav-Kaf. And when he says "LeChol Chai Ratzon," he should intend to draw down flow, sustenance, and abundant blessing to all the worlds. And when concluding the first blessing on Shabbat, he should further intend, in mentioning God's name in the blessing, the spelling of the Tetragrammaton with the filling of Yudin — that is, Yud-Vav-Dalet, Heh-Yud, Vav-Yud-Vav, Heh-Yud — and he should further intend the filling of the Yud itself, thus: Yud-Vav-Dalet, as mentioned in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, zal.

clarification.explanation: In the first blessing one begins "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who nourishes us and the entire world in His goodness," and so reads the Rashash, "HaEl," etc. When he says "Poteach et Yadecha," he should intend, in the initial letters (Poteach Et Yadecha), the holy name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei by numerical value, and likewise in the final letters (Chet-Tav-Kaf), by the At-Bash cipher, the same name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei; and in the word "UMasbi'a" he should intend that it equals numerically Chet-Tav-Kaf. And when he says "LeChol Chai Ratzon," he should intend to draw down flow, sustenance, and abundant blessing to all the worlds. And in concluding the blessing on Shabbat he should add the intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the spelling of the Yudin (Yud-Vav-Dalet Heh-Yud Vav-Yud-Vav Heh-Yud), and further intend the spelling of the Yud itself (Yud-Vav-Dalet).
takeaways: First blessing: "who nourishes us and the entire world in His goodness"
In "Poteach et Yadecha" one intends, in both the initial and final letters, the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei, and in "UMasbi'a" one intends the numerical value Chet-Tav-Kaf
On Shabbat one adds the intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the spelling of the Yudin and in the spelling of the Yud

paragraphs: In the second blessing one should begin "Nodeh Lecha" ("We thank You"), etc. And in the siddurim and in Simchat HaRegel it is written "Ve'al Chayim UMazon She'Atah Zan UMefarnes Otanu" ("and for life and sustenance, which You feed and provide for us"), but in Chesed La'alafim it is written thus: "Ve'al Chayim SheChonantanu Ve'al HaMazon She'Atah Zan," etc. ("and for life which You have granted us, and for the sustenance which You provide," etc.), and this version appears more correct. And he should say "Al HaKol" without the letter vav. And in concluding the second blessing, he should add, on Shabbat, the intention of mentioning God's name in the Tetragrammaton with the filling of Samech-Gimel — thus: Yud-Vav-Dalet, Heh-Yud, Vav-Aleph-Vav, Heh-Yud — and he should further intend the filling "Heh-Yud Yud," as mentioned in the siddur of the Rashash, zal.

clarification.explanation: In the second blessing of Birkat HaMazon one begins "Nodeh Lecha." In the siddurim and in the book Simchat HaRegel it is written "Ve'al Chayim UMazon She'Atah Zan UMefarnes Otanu," but in Chesed La'alafim the text is "Ve'al Chayim SheChonantanu Ve'al HaMazon She'Atah Zan," etc., and this version appears more correct; and he should say "Al HaKol" without the vav. And in concluding the second blessing he should add, on Shabbat, the intention of mentioning God's name — the Tetragrammaton — in the filling of Samech-Gimel (Yud-Vav-Dalet, Heh-Yud, Vav-Aleph-Vav, Heh-Yud), and further intend the filling "Heh-Yud Yud," as brought in the siddur of the Rashash, zal.
takeaways: The precise text of the second blessing: "Ve'al Chayim SheChonantanu Ve'al HaMazon She'Atah Zan," and "Al HaKol" without the vav.
On Shabbat, at the conclusion — intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the filling of Samech-Gimel (per the siddur of the Rashash).

paragraphs: In the third blessing one should begin "Rachem Hashem Elokeinu," etc., and one should also be careful to say "Re'enu Zunenu" ("feed us, sustain us") and not, as is written [in some texts], "Ro'enu Zunenu." He should also say "VeNa Al Tatzricheinu Hashem Elokeinu Lidei Matnot Basar VaDam," etc., "Yehi Ratzon SheLo Neivosh," etc. And in "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu" he should say "Nishbot Bo VeNanuach Bo VeNit'anag Bo" ("we shall rest on it, and be tranquil on it, and delight on it"), and he should say "VeGam She'achalnu VeShatinu" ("and also that we have eaten and drunk") and not say "Ve'af." And even on Shabbat, one must say, before the concluding blessing, "VeTivneh Yerushalayim Ir HaKodesh Bimheirah VeYameinu, Baruch Atah Hashem Boneh Yerushalayim." And although some read "Boneh BeRachamav" ("who builds in His mercy"), it is better to refrain than to add — one should not say "BeRachamav," as mentioned by the Acharonim. And in concluding this blessing on Shabbat, he should add the intention of the name of the conclusion in the filling of the Alfin — that is, Yud-Vav-Dalet Heh-Alef Vav-Alef Heh-Alef — and he should further intend the filling Vav-Yud-Vav, Yud-Vav-Dalet, Vav-Yud-Vav, as mentioned in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, zal. And after this concluding blessing of "Boneh Yerushalayim," one should answer "Amen" after his own blessing, since it is the conclusion of the blessings that are from the Torah, for the fourth blessing is rabbinic.

clarification.explanation: In the third blessing one begins "Rachem Hashem Elokeinu," and says "Re'enu Zunenu" (not "Ro'einu"), "VeNa Al Tatzricheinu Hashem Elokeinu Lidei Matnot Basar VaDam," and on Shabbat "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu... Nishbot Bo VeNanuach Bo VeNit'anag Bo," "VeGam She'achalnu VeShatinu" (not "Ve'af"). Even on Shabbat, one says before the conclusion "VeTivneh Yerushalayim Ir HaKodesh Bimheirah VeYameinu, Baruch Atah Hashem Boneh Yerushalayim," and should not say "Boneh BeRachamav" (it is better to refrain than to add). On Shabbat one adds, at the conclusion, the intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the filling of the Alfin. And after the conclusion "Boneh Yerushalayim," one answers "Amen" after his own blessing, since it is the conclusion of the blessings that are from the Torah (the fourth blessing being rabbinic).
takeaways: Third blessing: precise wording, and on Shabbat "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu" before "Boneh Yerushalayim"
One answers "Amen" after "Boneh Yerushalayim," since it is the conclusion of the Torah blessings

paragraphs: In the fourth blessing one should intend that he is prepared to fulfill a rabbinic commandment by reciting a rabbinic blessing, and through this preparatory intention there will be power in his intention in this blessing to raise up mayin nukvin and to draw down four lights of mochin to the aspect of Yaakov and Rachel, as mentioned in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, zal. And when he begins this blessing on Shabbat, he should add the intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the blessing, in the filling of the Heh-Heh's, that is, Yud-Vav-Dalet Heh-Heh Vav-Alef-Vav Heh-Heh, and should further intend the filling Heh-Yud Yud, as mentioned there. And the correct text to say is: "Hu Heitiv Lanu, Hu Meitiv Lanu, Hu Yeitiv Lanu; Hu Gemalanu, Hu Gomleinu, Hu Yigmeleinu" ("He has done good for us, He does good for us, He will do good for us; He has bestowed favor upon us, He bestows favor upon us, He will bestow favor upon us") — and this text follows the pattern of "was, is, and will be," and one should not say the text arranged on the pattern "King, King, will reign," as it appears in the siddur of our teacher the Rashash, zal. And there you will find intentions for every single word of this blessing, which is not the case in the other blessings — and from this you may understand the special quality of this blessing. And if, out of haste, one omits one of these words, or slurs over them, he loses much good; and one who is careful about this shall have the blessing of good come upon him.

clarification.explanation: In the fourth blessing one should intend that he is prepared to fulfill a rabbinic positive commandment by reciting a rabbinic blessing, and through this preparatory intention there will be power in his intention in this blessing to raise up mayin nukvin and to draw down four lights of mochin to the aspect of "Yaakov and Rachel" (as explained in the siddur of the Rashash). And when he begins this blessing on Shabbat, he should add the intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in the blessing, in the filling of the Heh-Heh's — that is, Yud-Vav-Dalet Heh-Heh Vav-Alef-Vav Heh-Heh — and should further intend an additional filling: Heh-Yud Yud. And the correct text to say is: "Hu Heitiv Lanu, Hu Meitiv Lanu, Hu Yeitiv Lanu; Hu Gemalanu, Hu Gomleinu, Hu Yigmeleinu" — this text is built on the pattern of "was, is, and will be," and one should not say the text built on the pattern "King, King, will reign," as it appears in the siddur of the Rashash. And there, intentions are explained for every single word of this blessing, unlike the other blessings — from which one may understand its special elevated quality. And one who, out of haste, omits one of these intentions, or slurs over the text instead of saying it properly, loses much good; and one who is careful about this shall have the blessing of good come upon him.
takeaways: In the fourth blessing one should intend that it fulfills a rabbinic positive commandment.
On Shabbat one adds intention of the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei in two fillings: the filling of the Heh-Heh's (Yud-Vav-Dalet Heh-Heh Vav-Alef-Vav Heh-Heh) and the filling Heh-Yud Yud.
The correct text: "Hu Heitiv Lanu Hu Meitiv Lanu Hu Yeitiv Lanu, Hu Gemalanu Hu Gomleinu Hu Yigmeleinu" — not the text "King, King, will reign."
One who rushes and omits or slurs part of the text or the intention loses much good; one should take care to say it in full.

paragraphs: When the one who is blessing says "HaRachaman," everyone seated is obligated to answer "Amen" after each and every petition of "HaRachaman," as "Chesed La'alafim," Siman 215, letter 4, wrote. And although it is not forbidden to interrupt for these supplications of "HaRachaman," nevertheless it is forbidden to interrupt with mundane conversation. And one who blesses over a cup is under an even greater obligation not to interrupt between Birkat HaMazon and the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen" over the cup; see Mishbetzot Zahav, Siman 189, and Mayim HaChayim, Siman 5; examine them there, and other Acharonim. And when he says "HaRachaman," "He shall bless each and every one of us," if there are gentiles sitting there, he should say "each and every one of us, members of the covenant." And when he says "HaRachaman Hu Yita Torato," etc., he should add "VeYihyu Kol Ma'aseinu LeShem Shamayim" ("and may all our actions be for the sake of Heaven"). And the guest should be careful to bless the host, for this is an enactment of the Sages, and whoever blesses is blessed. And if the host is not making the meal for the guests in his own home, the guest should say "He shall bless the master of this meal." And if there are many hosts, who are brothers or partners in this meal, he should say "He shall bless the masters of this meal," and should say "with children who shall live and possessions that shall increase"; see Kaf HaChayim. And at a bridegroom's meal he should bless the groom and bride, and at a circumcision meal he should bless the child who was circumcised, by name, etc. Also, when he says "HaRachaman Hu Yefarnesenu BeKavod VeLo BeVizui," etc., he should not say "BeHeter VeLo Be'Isur" ("with permission and not with prohibition"), for surely the Holy One, blessed be He, will provide for him with permission and not with prohibition, and how could one say this in a manner of petition, requesting this of God, as if it were in doubt? And likewise he should be careful regarding the petition for livelihood recited on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

clarification.explanation: When the one blessing says "HaRachaman," all those seated are obligated to answer "Amen" after every petition. Although it is not forbidden to interrupt for these petitions of "HaRachaman," it is forbidden to interrupt them with mundane conversation, and one who blesses over a cup must be careful not to interrupt between Birkat HaMazon and the blessing "Borei Peri HaGafen." In "HaRachaman Hu Yevarech Kol Echad Ve'Echad Mimenu," if gentiles are present, he should say "each and every one of us, members of the covenant." The guest should be careful to bless the host, since this is an enactment of the Sages, and whoever blesses is blessed, using the appropriate wording for the occasion (the master of the meal, the groom and bride, the child who was circumcised). And in "HaRachaman Hu Yefarnesenu BeKavod," he should not say "BeHeter VeLo Be'Isur," since it is not fitting to request, as a matter of petition, something that God will certainly do in any case.
takeaways: One answers "Amen" after every "HaRachaman"; the guest blesses the host
One does not interrupt with mundane conversation, and does not say "BeHeter VeLo Be'Isur"

paragraphs: At the four meals of Shabbat, and likewise on Yom Tov, Chol HaMo'ed, and Rosh Chodesh, one says "Migdol" with a vav. And Chesed La'alafim wrote in the name of Rabbi David Pardo, zal, that at a circumcision meal as well it is fitting to say "Migdol" with a vav, according to the esoteric tradition; examine it there. And in the handwritten book Keter Malchut it is stated that at a Purim meal as well one should say "Migdol" with a vav, on account of that illumination revealed on that day, which is constant throughout the entire day. And at the very end one should say the verse "Oseh Shalom Bimromav," etc., intending in the initial letters of "Oseh Bimromav" the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei of the seventy-two-name expansion with Yudin, as mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, zal, in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, Parashat Eikev.

clarification.explanation: At the four meals of Shabbat — and likewise on Yom Tov, Chol HaMo'ed, and Rosh Chodesh — one says "Magdol" with a vav (not "Magdil"). And Chesed La'alafim wrote in the name of Rabbi David Pardo, zal, that at a circumcision meal as well it is fitting to say "Magdol" with a vav, according to the esoteric tradition; and in the handwritten book Keter Malchut it is stated that at a Purim meal as well one should say "Magdol" with a vav, on account of that illumination revealed on that day, which is constant throughout the entire day. And at the very end one says the verse "Oseh Shalom Bimromav," etc., intending in the initial letters "Oseh Bimromav" the name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei of the seventy-two-name expansion with Yudin — as brought in the words of our teacher the Ari, zal, in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, Parashat Eikev.
takeaways: On Shabbat, Yom Tov, Chol HaMo'ed, Rosh Chodesh — and also at a circumcision and at Purim (according to the esoteric tradition) — one says "Magdol" with a vav.
At the conclusion one says "Oseh Shalom Bimromav" and intends in the initial letters "Oseh Bimromav" the name of the seventy-two-name expansion with Yudin.

paragraphs: On Shabbat one says in the third blessing "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu," and the meaning of "HeChelitzanu" is "strengthen us." On Yom Tov, Chol HaMo'ed, and Rosh Chodesh one says at this point "Ya'aleh VeYavo," and does not mention Shabbat in "Ya'aleh VeYavo." And if he erred and did not mention Shabbat at the evening meal or the first meal of the day: if he remembers when he has said "Baruch Atah Hashem" before saying "Boneh Yerushalayim," he should conclude "Lamdeini Chukecha" and then mention "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu." And if he remembers after saying "Boneh Yerushalayim" but before beginning the fourth blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," he says there this text: "Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech Ha'olam, She'natan Shabbatot Limnuchah Le'amo Yisrael Be'ahavah Le'ot ULivrit, Baruch Atah Hashem Mekadesh HaShabbat." And if he does not know the text of this blessing, he should return to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon — it being sufficient for him to mention the special occasion, since he does not know how to correct the omission otherwise; but if he knows how to say the opening and closing of this blessing, that suffices even if he does not know the entire text properly. And if Yom Tov falls on Shabbat and he needed to say this text, he should say it thus: "Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech Ha'olam, She'natan Shabbatot Limnuchah Le'amo Yisrael Be'ahavah Le'ot ULivrit, VeYamim Tovim LeSasson ULeSimchah Et Yom Chag Ploni HaZeh, Baruch Atah Hashem Mekadesh HaShabbat VeYisrael VeHaZemanim." And the rule that this blessing suffices applies only when he remembered before beginning "HaTov VeHaMeitiv"; but if he did not remember until he had begun the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv," even if he has said only the word "Baruch," he returns to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon.

And if he erred at the third meal of Shabbat, there is a dispute: some say he returns [to the beginning] as in the law of the first and second meals, and some say he does not return. And although the strict law would require [following] the leniency that a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently, and thus he would not return, nevertheless, since according to the esoteric tradition we maintain that there is no difference in obligation between the third meal and the other two meals — they being equal in obligation — therefore one must rule that even at the third meal he returns. However, at another meal that one eats on the same day, after the morning meal at which he already blessed "HaMotzi" and Birkat HaMazon, all agree that if he erred there he does not return; see Birkei Yosef, Machazik Berachah, and Ikarei HaDat, Siman 13, letter 14.

clarification.explanation: On Shabbat one says in the third blessing "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu" ("HeChelitzanu" meaning "strengthen us"). On Yom Tov, Chol HaMo'ed, and Rosh Chodesh one says there "Ya'aleh VeYavo" (without mentioning Shabbat). And if he erred and did not mention Shabbat at the evening meal or the first meal of the day: if he remembers after saying "Baruch Atah Hashem" but before "Boneh Yerushalayim," he concludes "Lamdeini Chukecha" and says "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu"; and if he remembers after "Boneh Yerushalayim" but before the fourth blessing, he says the text "Baruch... She'natan Shabbatot Limnuchah... Baruch Atah Hashem Mekadesh HaShabbat" (and if Yom Tov falls on Shabbat he adds also "VeYamim Tovim LeSasson ULeSimchah" and mentions the holiday); and if he does not know this text, he returns to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon (it being sufficient to mention the essential opening and closing if he is not fluent in the entire text). And if he has already begun the blessing of "HaTov VeHaMeitiv" (even only the word "Baruch"), he returns to the beginning. And if he erred at the third meal of Shabbat — there is a dispute: some say he returns as in the law of the first two meals, and some say he does not return (since, strictly speaking, a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently). Yet we rule that he should return even at the third meal, since according to the esoteric tradition there is no difference in obligation between the third meal and the other two — they are equal in obligation. But if he erred at an additional meal eaten that day, after the morning meal at which he already blessed "HaMotzi" and Birkat HaMazon — all agree that he does not return.
takeaways: On Shabbat one says "Retzeh VeHachalitzeinu," and on Yom Tov/Chol HaMo'ed/Rosh Chodesh "Ya'aleh VeYavo," without mentioning Shabbat.

One who forgot to mention Shabbat has a precise order of correction depending on the stage at which he remembers, up to returning to the beginning of Birkat HaMazon if he has already begun the fourth blessing.

Erred at the third meal — the custom is to be stringent and return, even though strictly speaking some are lenient, on account of the kabbalistic teaching that the three meals are equal in obligation.
At an additional meal on that day which is not one of the three primary meals — all agree that he does not return even if he erred.

paragraphs: If he erred on Yom Tov — although the poskim wrote, and so wrote Maran, zal, that he returns as in the law of erring on Shabbat — nevertheless, since some say that one does not return on Yom Tov, we maintain that a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently, and he does not return on Yom Tov, except on the first night of Pesach and the first night of Sukkot; see Chesed La'alafim, Siman 189, and what is written there in the name of Moshe Yedaber, Siman 1; examine it there.

clarification.explanation: If one erred and did not mention Yom Tov, although the poskim (and Maran as well) wrote that he returns as in the law of Shabbat, nevertheless, since some say that one does not return on Yom Tov, we follow the rule that a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently, and he does not return on Yom Tov — except on the first night of Pesach and the first night of Sukkot (when there is an obligation to eat bread, and therefore he does return).
takeaways: Erred on Yom Tov: he does not return (a doubt regarding blessings is treated leniently)
Except on the first night of Pesach and Sukkot, when he does return

paragraphs: One who was eating and Shabbat departed [during the meal] mentions Shabbat in Birkat HaMazon, since we follow the beginning of the meal; and although some say we follow the present moment, the law is not so — and so is the widespread custom, to mention Shabbat, except that he should omit the word "HaZeh" ("this"). And if he erred and did not mention it, he does not return. The same law applies to Yom Tov, since here too we follow the beginning of the meal. But regarding Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah, although there is a dispute about this as well, we instruct that he should not mention them. And if he prayed the evening service in the middle of the meal, even on Shabbat, he does not mention it.

And regarding what we said, that on Shabbat, if the meal continued [into the next day], he mentions it — nevertheless, if the food he ate on Shabbat has already been digested, he does not mention it. And if Rosh Chodesh falls on Motza'ei Shabbat (the night after Shabbat), he mentions only Shabbat, since the two are contradictory to each other. And in the final blessing recited over the cup of Birkat HaMazon, he does not mention Shabbat. Likewise, if at the house of a groom the meal continued until the eighth night, he does not recite the Sheva Berachot over the cup of Birkat HaMazon, as mentioned in Chesed La'alafim, Siman 189, letter 7.

clarification.explanation: One who was eating and Shabbat departed in the middle of his meal mentions Shabbat in Birkat HaMazon, since we follow the beginning of the meal; and although some say we follow the present moment, the halachah is not so, and the widespread custom is to mention Shabbat — except that he omits the word "HaZeh." And if he erred and did not mention it, he does not return. The same applies to Yom Tov (we follow the beginning of the meal). But regarding Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah — although there is a dispute about these as well — we instruct that he should not mention them. And if he prayed the evening service in the middle of the meal, even on Shabbat, he does not mention it. And what we said, that on Shabbat, if the meal continued, he mentions it — that applies specifically if the food he ate on Shabbat has not yet been digested; but if it has been digested, he does not mention it. And if Rosh Chodesh falls on Motza'ei Shabbat, he mentions only Shabbat, since these are two contradictory matters. And in the final blessing recited over the cup of Birkat HaMazon, he does not mention Shabbat; and likewise, if at the groom's house the meal continued until the eighth night, he does not recite the Sheva Berachot over the cup of Birkat HaMazon (Chesed La'alafim).
takeaways: Shabbat/Yom Tov departed during the meal — he mentions it (following the beginning of the meal), but omits "HaZeh"; if he erred, he does not return.
Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah — one does not mention them; if he prayed the evening service in the middle, he does not mention it even on Shabbat.
If the food has been digested — he does not mention it; Rosh Chodesh on Motza'ei Shabbat — only Shabbat is mentioned; on the cup of Birkat HaMazon one does not mention Shabbat or Sheva Berachot.
